source.title: Does Bigger Mean Funnier? Evaluating Humor Generation Across the Qwen3 Model Family

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether model scale predicts a downstream capability using humor-generation evaluations rather than held-out pretraining loss or the original scaling-law measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws but does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws, or test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation. Its results on judge positional and length bias are evaluation diagnostics, not scaling outcomes.
record.test_reason: It applies V6 to a new setting, humor generation by Qwen3 models from 8B to 235B. It reports judge win rates and human ranks by model size, but measures no loss and fits no power law. T3 suits this better than T2: the method is not aimed at the original loss-scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find a consistent but non-significant human trend with size overall, and a significant preference for the largest model on high-agreement themes. They warn that the judge's perfect scaling correlation rests on positional and length biases.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates instruction-tuned model outputs on a downstream humor task using pairwise judge ratings and human rankings; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Human results depend on theme subset: the aggregate and low-agreement results are non-significant, while the high-agreement subset is significant. The automated judge has reported positional and length biases.

fits_no_version.finding: The LLM judge shows 73.5% positional bias and 62.2% length bias, and only 52.7% of transposed pairs give consistent winners.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The apparent downstream scaling trend on subjective tasks depends on LLM-judge artifacts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2nd Workshop on Computational Humor (CHum 2026)
record.problems: Only one joke per model per theme was generated, so within-model variance was not assessed. The dataset is relatively small; the automated evaluation uses one judge, with inter-judge reliability untested. Human ratings cover only three of five models, with 12 annotators and low agreement. The automated judge shows substantial positional and length biases.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested version were left out. Judge positional/length bias findings and qualitative joke examples are not separate scaling outcomes.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit.
No variation of depth or width at fixed parameter count. The dense vs MoE comparison does not hold parameter count fixed.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Untested: prediction from pretraining loss, any quantitative fit or forecast of task performance, tasks other than humor, and human ratings for 8B and 14B.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: Judge reliability: 52.7% of transposed pairs give consistent winners (p=0.12 vs chance). Positional bias is 73.5%; length bias is 62.2%. Both bear on how far R1–R5 can be read as a scaling result.
Each human annotator group independently ranks 235A22 first (1.88 and 1.92).
Per-theme winners on the high-agreement subset: 235A22 wins 9 of 22, 32B 8, 30A3 4.

record.verdict_notes: The sizes span only about 1.5 orders of magnitude in total parameters. Human ratings cover the three largest models only, and the MoE models confound total with active parameters. The high-agreement subset was defined after seeing the data. The study cites Kaplan et al. but is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation or parameter/token growth trends are tested.
The study compares dense and MoE models but does not vary depth, width, or architecture at a fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
The study evaluates humor generation but does not test whether a power-law form holds beyond text pretraining or in other training regimes.

It tests humor-generation quality across five model sizes within one family, with human ratings for only three models. It does not test other downstream tasks or predict performance from pretraining loss.
No scaling-law exponents or fit-dependence are examined.

rows.subject: 8B
rows.operation_detail: Generated one joke per theme and evaluated it in pairwise comparisons by DeepSeek-V3.2.
rows.note: Win rates increase monotonically across the five models (Spearman ρ = 1.0, p < 0.001), but the paper cautions that judge bias and overlapping uncertainty for mid-sized models limit interpretation as humor quality.
rows.check: This row is one point of a monotonic size trend (ρ=1.0), so the trend itself is observed. The paper attributes the trend partly to judge positional and length bias, and only 52.7% of transposed pairs give consistent winners.

rows.subject: 14B
rows.operation_detail: Generated one joke per theme and evaluated it in pairwise comparisons by DeepSeek-V3.2.
rows.note: The paper reports monotonically increasing judge win rates with total parameter count, but warns that judge artifacts may distort quality differences.
rows.check: Part of the monotonic judge trend (ρ=1.0). The mid-sized models' cluster-bootstrap CIs overlap.

rows.subject: 32B
rows.operation_detail: Generated one joke per theme and evaluated it in pairwise comparisons by DeepSeek-V3.2.
rows.note: The three mid-sized models cluster between 49–55%, and their 95% confidence intervals frequently overlap.
rows.check: Part of the monotonic judge trend. CIs overlap with 14B and 30A3.

rows.subject: 30A3
rows.operation_detail: Generated one joke per theme and evaluated it in pairwise comparisons by DeepSeek-V3.2.
rows.note: The judge's rating is close to 32B despite 3B active parameters per token; the paper also reports substantial judge positional and length biases.
rows.check: Ordered by total parameters (30B); by active parameters (3B) it would rank lowest. CIs overlap with neighbouring models.

rows.subject: 235A22
rows.operation_detail: Generated one joke per theme and evaluated it in pairwise comparisons by DeepSeek-V3.2.
rows.note: The judge shows a perfect monotonic ranking by total parameter count, but the paper cautions that the judge's biases may overstate differences.
rows.check: Top of the monotonic judge ranking, with the same judge-bias caveat.

rows.subject: 235A22
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators independently ranked anonymized jokes.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals overlap substantially; exact interval not stated
rows.note: This is the best aggregate mean rank among the three rated models, but the aggregate Friedman test is non-significant (χ² = 3.73, p = 0.155); pairwise tests all have p > 0.10.
rows.check: Among humans the aggregate model difference is non-significant (Friedman p=0.155, all pairwise p>0.10). The rule makes a non-significant difference absent, not partial.

rows.subject: 32B
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators independently ranked anonymized jokes.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals overlap substantially; exact interval not stated
rows.note: The aggregate human comparison among models is non-significant (Friedman p = 0.155); pairwise tests all have p > 0.10.
rows.check: Aggregate human difference is non-significant; the CI includes chance (2.0).

rows.subject: 30A3
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators independently ranked anonymized jokes.
rows.uncertainty: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals overlap substantially; exact interval not stated
rows.note: The aggregate human comparison among models is non-significant (Friedman p = 0.155); pairwise tests all have p > 0.10.
rows.check: Aggregate human difference is non-significant; the CI includes chance (2.0).

rows.subject: 235A22
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators ranked jokes on themes meeting the pairwise winner-agreement threshold.
rows.uncertainty: Friedman χ² = 6.47, p = 0.039; Kendall’s W = 0.025; pairwise Wilcoxon against 30A3: p = 0.020
rows.note: The largest model has the best mean rank on this subset; the significant pairwise result is against 30A3.
rows.check: The omnibus test is significant (p=0.039), but the effect is small (Kendall's W=0.025) and the only significant pair is 235A22 vs 30A3. The 22-theme subset was chosen after the fact by annotator agreement.

rows.subject: 32B
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators ranked jokes on themes meeting the pairwise winner-agreement threshold.
rows.note: The mean ranks order the models 235A22, 32B, then 30A3 on the high-agreement subset.
rows.check: 32B (dense) beats 30A3 (MoE) despite fewer total parameters, which is not significant (p=0.259). The ordering therefore follows active rather than total parameters.

source_check.correct: The ancillary verdict-fix explanation should say: 32B has more total parameters than 30A3 (32B versus 30B); the high-agreement mean-rank ordering follows total parameter count. It does not follow active parameter count: 235A22 has 22B active parameters, fewer than dense 32B. The 32B versus 30A3 difference is nonsignificant (p=0.259).
source_check.problem: The row fields are correct, but its verdict-fix explanation reverses the total-parameter comparison and incorrectly asserts ordering by active parameters.

rows.subject: 30A3
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators ranked jokes on themes meeting the pairwise winner-agreement threshold.
rows.uncertainty: Friedman χ² = 6.47, p = 0.039; Kendall’s W = 0.025; pairwise Wilcoxon against 235A22: p = 0.020
rows.note: The largest model significantly outperforms this model on the high-agreement subset.
rows.check: Significantly worse than 235A22 (p=0.020). Its gap to 32B is not significant.

rows.subject: 235A22
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators ranked jokes on themes below the pairwise winner-agreement threshold.
rows.note: The paper reports no model effect on this subset; all three mean ranks are within 0.07 of 2.0.
rows.check: No model effect in this subset (p=0.839).

rows.subject: 32B
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators ranked jokes on themes below the pairwise winner-agreement threshold.
rows.note: The paper reports no model effect on this subset; all three mean ranks are within 0.07 of 2.0.
rows.check: No model effect in this subset (p=0.839).

rows.subject: 30A3
rows.operation_detail: Human annotators ranked jokes on themes below the pairwise winner-agreement threshold.
rows.note: The low-agreement subset does not show a scaling-ordered ranking; the omnibus test reports no model effect.
rows.check: No model effect; 30A3 has the nominally best rank (1.972) here.

relationships.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 pairwise judge, five Qwen3 models, 50 themes
relationships.reason: Judge win rate rises monotonically with total parameters, 33.5% to 61.0% (ρ=1.0) (R1–R5). The authors attribute this partly to positional and length bias.
relationships.display_finding: Judge win rates increased monotonically from 33.5% to 61.0% with ρ=1.0, partly attributed to positional and length bias.

relationships.reason: There is no significant human difference between models (p=0.155; R6–R8), so the size trend depends on the choice of judge.
